title: Profiling domestic water bacteriome within the rainwater harvesting-dependent community of Carriacou Island, Grenada in the Southern Caribbean
content:
by Akilah T. M. Stewart, Adrian Cashman, John Agard, Dave Chadee, Adesh Ramsubhag

There have only been few studies utilizing next generation sequencing technologies for assessing microbial communities of domestic water in the Caribbean. In the current study, Illumina sequencing of the V4 region of 16S rRNA gene amplicons was used to profile the bacteriome of domestic water utilized by residents of Carriacou, Grenada. Analysis of 184 water samples resulted in a total of 11,472 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) that were dominated by Proteobacteria (52.2%) and Bacteroidota (15.5%). The families Comamonadaceae and Pedosphaeraceae were the most abundant in harvested rainwater stored in both cisterns and tanks. Nostocaceae and Gemmataceae dominated in protected borehole samples and Methylophilaceae and Gallionellaceae in open wells. Genera of potential public health importance were detected at varying prevalence levels, including Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas in rainwater stored in both cisterns and tanks. Amplicons of Escherichia-Shigella were detected in 12.6% of all samples. The detection of non-cultured bacteria via 16S rRNA gene sequencing cannot be used as a specific measure of risk. However, this study shows the occurrence of potential microbial hazards in domestic water in Carriacou that require further investigation. This is the first detailed study to profile the bacteriome of domestic water on a Caribbean island, specifically focusing on harvested rainwater from a rural community across two seasons. Further studies including the use of qPCR for increased data resolution are recommended for assessing risks to inhabitants to guide decisions on managing the microbiological quality of domestic water locally.
author: Akilah T. M. Stewart
